title: The Arithmetic of Lying Awake
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] There's a specific torment reserved for insomniacs who also happen to be analytically minded, since we insist on quantifying the very thing sabotaging us.
Narrator: Lying there at half past two, I'd calculate precisely how many hours of sleep remained possible, as though the arithmetic itself might somehow induce drowsiness.
Narrator: [carefully] It never did, obviously. If anything, the calculation functioned as its own stimulant, alertness disguised as diligence, a mind convinced it was solving something.
Narrator: What I eventually understood, after months of this, is that the anxiety about sleeplessness had become entirely separable from whatever originally caused the sleeplessness.

Narrator: [reflective] The original stressor might resolve itself completely, and still the ritual would persist, since the fear had metastasized into fearing the insomnia rather than whatever preceded it.
Narrator: A sleep specialist I eventually consulted described this with a phrase I've never forgotten: the bed had become the scene of the crime rather than a place of rest.

Narrator: [honestly] My nervous system, she explained, had quietly learned to associate the mattress itself with vigilance, an association built entirely through repetition rather than conscious choice.
Narrator: The prescribed remedy felt almost insultingly simple: leave the bed entirely if sleep hadn't arrived within twenty minutes, breaking the association one deliberate exit at a time.
Narrator: [gently] I resisted this advice initially, since abandoning the bed felt like conceding defeat rather than strategic retreat, a distinction that mattered more to my pride than my sleep.
Narrator: Reluctantly trying it, I found something counterintuitive happened: the nights improved not because I forced sleep, but because I finally stopped negotiating with it so aggressively.
Narrator: [calmly] Months later, the calculating mind still occasionally surfaces at odd hours, though I've learned to treat its arrival as information rather than emergency.
Narrator: Sleep, it turns out, resembles trust more than it resembles a task; both dissolve the moment you try to seize them by force.
